qrdBas-a19815-d1e101.summary: Rubric for the eighth prologue question of Book 1.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e110.summary: States the question: whether theology is practical or speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e121.summary: First argument that theology is speculative: Boethius (De trinitate) lists theology among the three speculative sciences, its subject being the first substance lacking matter, God.
claims: Boethius classes theology as speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e139.summary: Second: some speculative science is nobler than any practical one (Metaphysics I), so the noblest science is speculative, and theology is noblest.
claims: The noblest science is speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e149.summary: Third: science of eternal, immobile substance is speculative (Metaphysics VI), being of what is not operable by the knower, and theology is of God.
claims: Science of eternal immobile substance is speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e160.summary: Fourth: this science was found when the necessities of life were available and to flee ignorance, since concern for necessities impedes it (Metaphysics I), so it is speculative. The last words introduce the counter-argument.
claims: Science pursued for its own sake once necessities are met is speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e176.summary: Against: a science seeking something beyond truth and speculation is practical, not speculative (Avicenna, Metaphysics I.7); theology is such, since love is the fulfilment of the law (Romans 13), the end of the precept is charity (1 Timothy), the whole law hangs on the two commandments (Matthew 22), and Augustine says whoever keeps charity holds all that is open and hidden in Scripture.
claims: Theology aims beyond truth, at charity, so it is practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e200.summary: Second: a science that is 'so that we may become good' and is the science of divine law is practical (Ethics II); theology is such.
claims: Theology as science of divine law aims at our becoming good.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e214.summary: First step: set out opinions and argue against them.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e222.summary: Second step: answer the question differently.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e227.summary: Third step: respond to the principal arguments.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e229.summary: Five opinions in general: theology is purely speculative, purely practical, both speculative and practical, affective, or contemplative.
claims: Five positions exist on theology's character.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e245.summary: Those holding theology purely speculative differ. First way: there are two acts of will, one perfecting the will (regarding the end, by which it unites itself to the ultimate end) and one perfected by it (regarding means, tending outward). The first needs no directive knowledge, only showing of the object, since the will is naturally determined regarding the end, and knowledge ordered to it is speculative. The second needs direction, which belongs to practical science. The act regarding means is not theology's end except as subordinate, and the act regarding the end is an extrinsic end in another power, from which theology is not called practical or speculative; it is called speculative from its proper intrinsic end, speculation of theological truth, not directive of the will's act about the end. So theology is speculative, since its principal act needs no direction.
claims: The will's act regarding the end needs only showing of the object, not direction.
Theology's principal intended act, love of the end, needs no directive knowledge.
Theology is speculative from its intrinsic end, contemplation of truth.
concepts: act of will regarding end and means

qrdBas-a19815-d1e343.summary: Arguments for this: Augustine's sermon on Jacob and Esau says all our works are to cleanse the mind's eye to see God, so our science is ordered to the vision of God, which is not directive. God's and the blessed's science is not directive, since no error is possible, so ours is not either. Faith is a speculative habit, succeeded by vision, so is the science of faith. If extension to love made science practical, all sciences would be, since every science issues in some affection.
claims: Our works aim at cleansing the mind's eye to see God.
Faith, succeeded by vision, is speculative.
Not every extension to affection makes knowledge practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e385.summary: So they say: however much theology extends to love of God as its end outside the genus of cognition, it cannot be called practical from that, but is speculative from its proper intrinsic end, its cognitive act, not directive in the volition of the end, purely speculative and ostensive of the object.
claims: Theology is purely speculative and ostensive regardless of its extension to love.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e404.summary: They prove that a habit cannot be called practical from an extrinsic end, but only from an end within the genus of cognition, truth in conformity with right appetite. The act perfecting the habit is its end, not one in another power; that act belongs to all and only those with the habit, while love of God can be had without theology; an act outside cognition is the proper intrinsic end of an appetitive or moral habit, not an intellectual one. So a habit is speculative from truth not directive of external operation, practical from its intrinsic good, truth in conformity with right appetite directing another power's operation (Ethics VI).
claims: A habit is named practical or speculative only from its intrinsic end within cognition.
Love of God can exist without theology, so it is not theology's proper end.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e472.summary: Second way: theology is purely speculative though it extends to love of God, and even if that love can be elicited rightly or wrongly so that theology directs it, since love of God is not truly praxis, not being about a contingent object. The Commentator (Ethics I) says praxis is operation according to choice, and choice and deliberation concern only contingents (Ethics III). Third way: no volition or act of will is properly praxis, or only in relation to an act commanded in a lower power, since all praxis follows choice, which is its effective principle, not praxis itself (Ethics VI; Commentator on Ethics I).
claims: Love of God is not praxis because it is not about a contingent object.
Praxis is operation according to choice; choice itself is not praxis.
Acts of will are praxis only in relation to commanded acts.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e535.summary: They prove specifically that meritorious love of God is not praxis: it is not in our natural power but requires a supernatural agent and habit; it is not about something contingent operable by us; and it is the principal thing in which the contemplative life consists (Isidore, Gregory on Ezekiel). So it is not praxis as philosophers understood it.
claims: Meritorious love of God is not in our natural power.
Love of God constitutes the contemplative life.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e555.summary: The author's replies: love of God is in our power, elicitively (the habit contributes nothing to the act's eliciting) or at least dispositively, as health is in the physician's power, though not completively, and medicine is still practical. Praxis need not concern a contingent object, though it often does. Love of God is more principal in our contemplative life than in the philosophers' account, yet is truly praxis; the saints' 'contemplative life' is not the philosophers' 'speculative life'.
claims: Love of God is in our power at least dispositively.
Praxis need not concern contingent objects.
The saints' contemplative life differs from the philosophers' speculative life.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e584.summary: So they say theology is not practical because it does not extend to true praxis, since no power below intellect and will can act regarding its object, God.
claims: No lower power can act regarding God.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e595.summary: These three ways all hold theology purely speculative though extending to love of God or the end, whether because the will is naturally determined to that love once the object is shown (first way), or because love of God is not praxis, not concerning a contingent object (second way), or because no act of will is praxis (third way).
claims: Three ways hold theology purely speculative for different reasons.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e627.summary: Against the first way's foundation: on their own view a science whose act directs praxis is practical. Though one cannot err in willing the end in universal, one can err in willing the end in particular, regarding the particular object and circumstances, so the will is not naturally determined to it. Theology shows the end in particular, so it directs that volition and is practical.
claims: One can err in willing the end in particular.
Theology shows the end in particular and so directs volition.
concepts: end in universal and in particular

qrdBas-a19815-d1e662.summary: Second: if love of something is principally intended outside the genus of cognition, cognition of it is principally intended within that genus (as they grant). Love of the end is so intended, so cognition of the end is principally intended within cognition, and the object principally intended in any science is its first object, so the end is theology's first object. Practical principles are taken principally from the end, so theology's principles are practical, and so are its conclusions, since principles and conclusions share the same genus.
claims: The end is theology's first object.
Principles taken from the end are practical, so theology's principles and conclusions are practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e693.summary: Against the claim that knowledge is practical from an intrinsic end within cognition: Metaphysics I says practical science is for use, speculative for knowing, so the end distinguishing them is outside cognition, use or operation. Metaphysics II: speculative's end is truth, practical's is work, for though practical considers truth it does not stop there; truth consists in cognition, so work is distinguished from cognition. If cognition were the end, practical science would be speculative. The paragraph closes by turning to the second way.
claims: Practical science's distinguishing end, use or work, lies outside cognition.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e728.summary: Against the second way (love of God in particular is not praxis because not about a contingent): all conditions of praxis apply to it; the first object of praxis need not be operable or contingent; and an operation to which a virtue inclines elicitively, as charity and naturally acquired friendship toward God consonant with right reason do, is truly praxis.
claims: Love of God meets all the conditions of praxis.
Charity inclines to love of God as to its praxis.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e761.summary: Confirmed: a human act properly in man's power and not belonging to the intellect is praxis, especially when directable. The last words turn to the third way.
claims: A directable human act in our power is praxis.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e777.summary: Against the third way, that the elicited act of will is not per se praxis: it was shown above that being praxis belongs first to the will's elicited act and to others only through it.
claims: The will's elicited act is first and per se praxis.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e789.summary: Against the claim that choice is not praxis but its cause: by Aristotle (Ethics VI-VII) choice is an operation directed by right reason, since there is no right choice without right reason and virtue; so choice is praxis, an operation outside cognition directed by right reason.
claims: Choice is praxis, as an operation directed by right reason.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e807.summary: Further: the operations from which moral virtue is generated are praxis, like the virtue's acts, and moral virtue is generated by frequent choices; so choices are praxis. Even if no lower power acted, choices alone would be praxis: one without money who often chooses to distribute it liberally, if he had it, would acquire the habit of liberality, the object being sufficiently present in phantasm.
claims: Moral virtue is generated by repeated choices, which are praxis.
Interior choices alone can generate virtue.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e844.summary: Further: a thing does not get its character from relation to its effect; choice or elicited volition relates to lower powers' acts as cause to effect, so it is not praxis by relation to them, rather the converse. The author does not hold these three ways, which rest on false foundations.
claims: Choice is not praxis by relation to commanded acts; rather they are praxis through it.
The three ways rest on false foundations.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e862.summary: Confirmed: the description of praxis fits choice, and Aristotle says the doable and the choosable are the same.
claims: The doable and the choosable are the same.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e871.summary: Reply to the first argument for the first way: all our works are to purify the mind's eye so that God may be seen or known, at least external works like fasting and vigils, and not only that he be seen but further that, seen, he be loved, which Augustine does not exclude.
claims: Our works aim at seeing and further at loving God.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e889.summary: Reply to the second: whether God's and the blessed's science is practical will be treated in the body of the question; in any case our will following our theology in via needs direction in many matters.
claims: Wayfarers' volition following theology needs direction.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e903.summary: Reply to the third: granted that faith and beatific vision are speculative, our theology is practical in some respects; and some say faith is a practical habit and vision practical, which will appear below.
claims: Even if faith is speculative, theology can be practical in part.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e921.summary: Reply to the last: not every extension to affection makes knowledge practical, only directive extension arising from appetite for the end; any knowledge directive of a praxis from appetite for the end is practical, not every knowledge.
claims: Only directive extension from appetite for the end makes knowledge practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e943.summary: Reply to the first argument for the second claim: the proper intrinsic end of any habit is its elicited act, but not always the whole principal end from which it is denominated, which may be an act of another power, as one who fornicates for gain is called avaricious rather than lustful from the principal end. So the proper, intrinsic, and principal end of practical science is not cognition of truth but operation of good outside cognition.
claims: A habit is denominated from its principal end, which may lie in another power.
Practical science's principal end is operation of the good outside cognition.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e967.summary: Reply to the second: it does not concern the principal end, which can be had without the practical habit, though not the proper intrinsic end elicited by the habit. Or one might say charitable love of God cannot be had without theology or something corresponding to faith or its conclusions.
claims: The principal end can be had without the habit; the proper elicited end cannot.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e985.summary: Reply to the third: the same act can be the per se intrinsic end of two habits differing in genus and species, but not uniformly: of one as immediate end elicited by it, of the other mediately, as charitable love is the end of charity and of theology. The good of the practical intellect is truth in conformity with appetite, but it is called practical not from its good but from its end outside intellect. The last words introduce the reply to the second way.
claims: One act can be the intrinsic end of two habits, immediately and mediately.
The practical intellect is named from its end outside intellect, not from its good.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1018.summary: Reply to the second way's authority: the Commentator's 'praxis is operation according to choice' is true of some praxis, not all; some praxis is not choice, though every choice is praxis.
claims: Every choice is praxis, but not every praxis is choice.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1037.summary: Reply to the third way's first argument (no elicited act of will is praxis except in relation to a commanded act): choice is the effective principle of the commanded act, but it does not follow that choice is not praxis, since it needs virtue and right reason as causes (Aristotle). Rather choice is first praxis, and the commanded act is praxis and good through it, when choice is right.
claims: Choice is first praxis; commanded acts are praxis through choice.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1063.summary: Reply to the second: commanded acts are indeed praxis, but choices are praxis first.
claims: Choices are praxis prior to commanded acts.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1070.summary: Reply to the third: as before; or the Commentator takes choice for the action of choosing, in the category of action, which is not properly praxis, while the elicited act itself, to which the eliciting relates as effective cause or production, is.
claims: The production of choice differs from the elicited act of choice.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1096.summary: Another opinion (Scotus): theology is simply practical, which different people prove differently.
claims: Theology is simply practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1103.summary: First proof: a science is practical whose first and principally intended conclusion is practical, 'God is to be loved' ('love the Lord your God with your whole heart'), which theology concludes from its first object, deity, by which God is lovable by nature. That this is theology's principal conclusion is shown by Augustine (whoever keeps charity holds all of Scripture) and 1 Timothy (the end of the precept is charity); it is practical, directing praxis, love of God.
claims: Theology's principal conclusion, that God is to be loved, is practical.
God is lovable from the ratio of deity.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1138.summary: Second: the science of divine law is simply practical, since law exists for directing good operation, promoting good and restraining evil; theology is such a science (James 1: 'be doers of the word, not hearers only').
claims: Theology as science of divine law is simply practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1161.summary: Third: knowledge aptitudinally conformable to right volition and naturally prior to it is simply practical, since it directs and regulates that volition, which is praxis. Our theology of necessary truths is such: its first object, God, virtually contains what volition must conform to, the principles of rectitude are taken from it, and it determines our intellect to determinate knowledge of necessary rectitude prior to any created will. So theology has both priority and conformity to praxis and is practical.
claims: Knowledge naturally prior and conformable to right volition is practical.
The principles of rectitude are taken from the divine object.
Theology has priority and conformity to praxis, the two marks of practical knowledge.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1203.summary: Fourth: theology's first object is the ultimate end, and principles taken from the ultimate end in a created intellect are necessarily practical, directing and virtually containing knowledge and praxis about means. So theology's principles and conclusions are practical, and it is simply practical and in no way speculative. The last words announce arguments against this opinion.
claims: Principles taken from the ultimate end are practical.
Theology is simply practical and in no way speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1227.summary: Against the 'simply practical' opinion's foundations (its conclusion is assessed later). First foundation: theology's principal cognition is practical from the ratio of its first object, God under deity. Against: as shown, no knowledge, conclusion, or principle is practical from the object as object, but from appetite for the end; so theology's principal conclusion is not practical from the ratio of its object.
claims: Knowledge is not practical from its object as object.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1253.summary: Second foundation: theology is the science of divine law, directive in operation. Against: as to what it principally considers, theology is not a science of divine law but of God's nature and perfection (that God is triune and one), with other things only by attribution; only in some part does it consider the moral doable good, the subject of divine law.
claims: Theology principally concerns God's nature and perfection, not divine law.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1282.summary: Third foundation: theology has a twofold extension to praxis (its object virtually contains praxis's rectitude and determines our intellect to know it naturally prior to praxis). Against the first point: being formally and actually practical cannot come from aptitudinal conformity to later praxis, since nothing actual comes from what is not actual; aptitudinal conformity and priority are only potential, or, if actual, relations of reason.
claims: Aptitudinal conformity and priority cannot make knowledge actually practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1317.summary: Against the second point (that this twofold relation comes principally from the object): what is indifferent to practical and speculative knowledge cannot make knowledge principally practical, and every object is such, since an intellect can consider any particular object with or without prior appetite for the end.
claims: Every object is indifferent between practical and speculative knowledge.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1342.summary: Further: if knowledge were practical because its object virtually contains rectitude, we could have no speculative knowledge, and Metaphysics XII would be practical; indeed we could have no speculative knowledge of any particular being, since each contains, as object, some rectitude of possible praxis about it and determines the intellect to know it.
claims: The object criterion would abolish speculative knowledge.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1373.summary: Further: God's knowledge of himself and the blessed's of God would be practical, being prior and conformable to God's volition and the blessed's fruition, which seems false. The same object can be known practically and speculatively: Aristotle (Ethics I.10) says the carpenter and the geometer both consider the straight line, one to work, one to know; the Commentator (Ethics VI and II) says different sciences concern the same object, and if different powers (intellect and will) can, so can different habits. Medicine divides into speculative and practical about the healable body. Since the object is an equivocal cause of science, this is no problem. It is very unfitting to say no speculative science of God is possible, as those who make theology purely practical from its object, like Scotus, seem to; God's and the blessed's theology are purely speculative.
claims: The object criterion would make God's self-knowledge practical.
The same object admits speculative and practical knowledge (carpenter and geometer, medicine).
It is unfitting to deny speculative knowledge of God, as Scotus seems to.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1454.summary: Objection: in God and the blessed there is praxis and conformity, but no possible error, so the knowledge is not directive. Reply: this is no help on their principles, though true in fact. As an agent intends form per se and removal of contraries only accidentally, a practical habit per se is conformable and prior to right volition and only accidentally excludes error where error is possible through the habit's imperfection. So on their view God's and the blessed's knowledge would still be practical, which is false.
claims: On Scotus's criteria, practicality does not depend on possibility of error.
Excluding error is accidental to a practical habit.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1491.summary: Fourth foundation: practical principles are taken from the end, and the end is theology's object. Against: if from the end as end, distinguished from object, this contradicts their claim that knowledge is practical from the object, and in that sense the end is not theology's first subject, since God is not its subject as desired or loved. If from the end as object, it is false, as shown. So the opinion, as proved, is not true in its foundations.
claims: The 'end as object' argument equivocates.
God is not theology's subject under the ratio of end.
concepts: end as end versus as object

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1533.summary: Third opinion: theology is both speculative and practical. Its proponents differ. One (Aquinas) holds that theology, though simply one, is both, since it extends under one formal ratio (as knowable by divine light) to what is considered in the philosophical sciences, some speculative and some practical, as divine science is one about God and about what he makes. It is more speculative than practical, since it treats divine things more principally than human acts, and treats human acts only as ordering man to the more perfect knowledge or vision of God, in which beatitude consists.
claims: Theology, though one, is both speculative and practical.
It is more speculative, treating human acts as ordered to the vision of God.
concepts: unity under the light of revelation

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1594.summary: Another, holding theology is not one habit but several, says it is speculative and practical by its different parts, as a science with some writings on law and some on philosophy, whether in separate books or interspersed, as Scripture mixes them.
claims: Theology is speculative and practical by its distinct parts.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1626.summary: Their proof: no purely speculative science treats action more distinctly than needed for speculation, nor any purely practical science treats speculables more distinctly than needed for action. Theology treats each as distinctly as if it concerned that alone, so it is neither purely practical nor purely speculative, but both.
claims: Theology treats speculables and doables with independent distinctness, so it is both.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1665.summary: Further: a science named from a multitude of objects, one merely speculable and another doable, cannot be called purely speculative or purely practical; theology is such.
claims: Theology's objects include both speculables and doables.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1678.summary: They also say it is more principally speculative: its nobler part concerns the nobler object, the eternal; the etymology 'discourse about God' shows it; and as speculative it agrees more with the ultimate end, the beatific vision. The paragraph closes by turning to arguments against the first variant.
claims: Theology is principally speculative by its nobler part, etymology, and the vision as end.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1702.summary: Against the first variant: one simply undivided habit cannot be speculative and practical, since practical habit is directive from appetite for the end and they are divided by contradiction; yet they hold theology is simply one habit by unity of formal ratio.
claims: One undivided habit cannot be both practical and speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1724.summary: Note: Thomas seems to contradict himself, holding in the same question of Summa I that God under the ratio of God is theology's subject and here that God as revealable is. Revealability is not the ratio of God but a relation of reason to the knower, on the knower's side, as sensible to sense. He argues theology's unity from revealability, but unity of science comes from the subject only as on the subject's side, the ratio causing the habit or act.
claims: Aquinas inconsistently assigns deity and revealability as theology's ratio.
Revealability is a relation to the knower, not the subject's ratio.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1766.summary: Hence it is false that theology, being one, is both: it would be practical about the eternal and speculative about the doable, being as one both of both. The example of divine science is not to the point: it is purely speculative, or infinite and unlimited, so practical and speculative can belong to it, while they divide by contradiction every finite habit.
claims: A finite habit cannot be both practical and speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1798.summary: Against the claim that theology is more speculative because principally ordered to vision: beatitude does not consist totally or principally in vision but in fruition and love, so theology is ordered more to love than to vision; and if ordering to love suffices for practicality, as both proponents seem to intend, theology would be more practical. The last words turn to the second variant.
claims: Beatitude consists principally in fruition and love, not vision.
Theology is ordered more to love than vision.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1831.summary: Against the second variant (several habits, speculative and practical by parts), though it is more fitting: its foundation is that theology is speculative and practical from diverse objects, one doable and contingent, the other necessary and eternal, so that it takes practicality principally from the object, which was disproved.
claims: Objects do not determine practicality.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1862.summary: Second, turning its own reason: a science treating nothing more distinctly than needed to direct praxis is practical, and theology is such, since everything in it (the eternal, the contingent, the particular end, its properties, means and effects) is necessary for directing praxis in which one could err without knowing them. So their minor is false, and the reason supports the opposite.
claims: Everything in theology is needed to direct praxis, so the argument supports practicality.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1891.summary: Third: a science as unified as geometry or arithmetic, though considering eternal and temporal, cannot be called speculative and practical from those objects; since they do not impede that unity, they do not prevent it from being purely speculative or purely practical, and theology is so unified.
claims: Diverse objects do not prevent a unified science from being purely one or the other.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1920.summary: Hence, though theology's principal object is eternal and names it, and the doable is less noble, it does not follow that theology is more speculative; it could be principally practical as directive of praxis from appetite for the end, since knowledge is practical or speculative from that end, not from the object.
claims: Nobility of object does not make theology more speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1946.summary: Against the claim that theology as speculative is more like the ultimate end, vision: the same argument as against the previous variant applies, since both mean the same. Ends the third opinion. The paragraph closes by introducing the view that theology is neither.
claims: The vision argument fails for the same reasons.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1960.summary: Against holding theology neither practical nor speculative: Aristotle (Metaphysics VI) says every science is speculative or practical.
claims: Every science is speculative or practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1971.summary: Second: practical and speculative divide knowledge sufficiently and essentially, as they divide intellect accidentally, so every scientific habit or act is speculative or practical.
claims: Practical and speculative exhaustively divide knowledge.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1987.summary: Third: either a science's end and good is truth in conformity with right appetite (Ethics VI), and it is practical, or not, and it is speculative.
claims: The dichotomy follows from conformity with right appetite.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e1996.summary: Fourth: either knowledge is directive of praxis from appetite for the end, and practical, or not, and speculative. The last words introduce the remaining two opinions.
claims: Knowledge either directs praxis from appetite for the end or not.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2005.summary: The opinions that theology is contemplative or affective are dismissed as plainly false on their proponents' intention, which is to assign members of knowledge other than speculative and practical, impossible as shown. If contemplative and affective were taken as falling under speculative and practical, there would be no difference in conclusion, but that does not seem their intent. Ends the first article.
claims: Contemplative and affective are not further members beyond speculative and practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2031.summary: Second article, answering the question: theology is distinguished as before into God's, the blessed's, and wayfarers'.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2045.summary: On God's theology (of necessary, contingent, or any truths), supposing as probable that praxis directable by practical knowledge belongs formally to the same subject as the practical knowledge: by Metaphysics VI practical knowledge concerns praxis whose principle is in the knower; the intellect is moved to practical knowledge by appetite for the end, so praxis and appetite belong to the same subject; and otherwise practical knowledge would lack per se priority and causality over praxis, since it first directs the will's elicited act in the knower and through it the commanded external act.
claims: Praxis directed by practical knowledge belongs to the same subject as the knowledge.
concepts: same subject of knowledge and praxis

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2089.summary: Note: every praxis in an external subject is commanded rather than elicited relative to it; the ratio of praxis belongs first to the elicited act, so a subject lacking an elicited act that is praxis has no praxis or practical knowledge, even if its knowledge directs some operation; such knowledge is speculative.
claims: Knowledge directing another's acts, without the knower's own elicited praxis, is speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2109.summary: Given this, all of God's knowledge is simply speculative. Knowledge that is not and cannot be directive of praxis intrinsic to the knower is not practical; no intrinsic divine praxis is directable, nor can God's practical power, the will, err, else he could sin; where error is impossible, direction would be posited in vain.
claims: God's knowledge is simply speculative.
God's will cannot err, so needs no direction.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2140.summary: Second, regarding God's knowledge of necessary truths: formally practical knowledge necessarily presupposes appetite for the end, but the divine essence as first object, with the intellect, suffices as motive to contain all divine knowledge of necessary truths, without the will or its act; so none of it is formally practical.
claims: God's knowledge of necessary truths does not depend on the will and is not practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2171.summary: Third: no knowledge is formally practical unless some praxis about the same object, free to elicit or not, can follow in the knower's power, since such praxis requires direction; but no divine praxis about necessary things is so in God's power, since God necessarily wills every necessary thing.
claims: God wills necessary things necessarily, so has no free praxis about them.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2195.summary: Fourth, regarding God's knowledge of contingents: knowledge posterior to all praxis in the knower is not formally practical, and God's knowledge of future contingents follows every act of his will (if there is praxis in God, which he doubts), since the will determines contingents before the intellect knows them. Objection: an executive power's productive act follows that knowledge and could be praxis. Reply: there is no third, executive power in God; producing ad extra is just willing this to be at a given time. Even if there were, its act could not be praxis, since God's elicited will-act, to which the ratio of praxis would first belong, is not praxis, and there is no possible error.
claims: God's knowledge of contingents follows his will and so is not practical.
God has no executive power distinct from will; producing is willing.
God's elicited will-act is not praxis.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2268.summary: Concludes that God's theology is speculative. Even granting, against the first supposition, that God's science extends to directing all secondary agents' praxis as their measure and rule, and arises from appetite for the end (his self-love), it remains purely speculative, since God's self-love is not formally praxis, being undirectable and incapable of error; knowledge not preceded by formal praxis cannot be formally practical. Knowledge of the ultimate end in particular is not formally practical either, since no praxis precedes it except perhaps volition of the end in universal, where error is impossible. On the view that practicality consists in priority and conformity to praxis, without requiring prior appetite, God's science could be called practical.
claims: God's theology is purely speculative even if it directs creatures' praxis.
God's self-love is not praxis, since it cannot err.
On Scotus's criteria God's science might be called practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2344.summary: The blessed's theology is likewise purely speculative: it does not direct any praxis from a prior appetite for the end that is formally praxis. Before their theology, the beatific vision, they have no volition that is praxis regarding the end in universal or in particular; vision precedes their volition of the end, and the love following vision is not praxis, since error is impossible, the act being necessarily right in object and circumstances.
claims: The blessed's theology is purely speculative.
Beatific love cannot err and so is not praxis.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2379.summary: Objection: the blessed's will as power can absolutely err, though not in the beatific act, so their knowledge directs the power and is practical. Reply: a power is directable only for its act, and cannot be directed or err without an act; in this act error is impossible. Even if it directed the power, the vision would not be practical, since it does not arise from appetite for the end preceding vision. Nor if knowledge and praxis need not belong to the same subject, and the blessed's theology directed some extrinsic praxis, would it be practical.
claims: Direction concerns acts, not powers in abstraction.
The beatific vision does not arise from prior appetite and so is not practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2427.summary: So for the blessed's theology, necessary or contingent (if they have any of contingents in the Word). Their other sciences in their own genus are another matter not pursued now, and likewise non-beatific theology in their own genus can be answered from the above.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2447.summary: Note: for knowledge to be practical it must direct, or be apt to direct, an operation in which error is possible, as to whether, how, or whether not to posit it; if no error is possible, knowledge cannot be directive or practical. Objection: excluding error is accidental to direction, so knowledge directive of itself suffices. Reply: knowledge cannot be directive while operation and power are not directable; though directive knowledge excludes error accidentally, per se it posits direction, which here it cannot. So God's and the blessed's knowledge is only ostensive of the object, not directive, hence speculative.
claims: Practical knowledge requires directing an operation in which error is possible.
God's and the blessed's knowledge is ostensive, not directive.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2495.summary: Objection: the blessed will can elicit fruition or not, sin and lose it, elicit it more or less intensely, or order it to another end, so it is directable. Reply: none of the first three is in its power (as will be said in Book IV), since the will has no such causality over the beatific act; ordering it to something other than God would not be a beatific act. And even if all were in its power, the vision would still not be directive from appetite for the end preceding it, so it remains speculative. The last words begin the treatment of wayfarers' abstractive theology.
claims: The beatified will cannot fail to elicit fruition or vary it.
The vision remains speculative regardless.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2544.summary: Wayfarers' possible abstractive theology would seem speculative, being infused by God and not in man's power, so not directive from appetite for the end, nor does appetite move the intellect to it. But if, once its principle (an infused species distinctly representing the divine essence) is had, a person could be moved by desire for the end to acts generating the habit, and so to a habit directing praxis about God, such as love, in which one can still err (not being beatific), it could probably be called practical. If the intellect is moved to it only by God infusing the species, the first answer holds.
claims: Possible abstractive theology is speculative if wholly infused.
It would be practical if its acts could be moved by desire for the end to direct fallible love of God.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2588.summary: Our theology, acquired by study aided by faith, is, in the author's present view, practical as a whole and in every part, though an aggregate of partial habits. Knowledge that, from appetite for the end (which is truly praxis), is by nature directive of some praxis is practical. Every learner of theology, acting according to theology's nature, is moved by desire and love of its end, God or more perfect charitable love of God, to study everything theology treats (end and means, necessary and contingent), so as to direct praxis about the ultimate end or means to be right and perfect. First he wills and loves God; then the will moves the intellect to theological knowledge directing love of God in due circumstances. So theology is simply practical.
claims: Our theology is practical as a whole and in every part.
The theologian studies from love of God in order to direct that love rightly.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2660.summary: Second: theology is speculative, practical, or both. Not purely speculative, since its principal end is not truth but charitable love directed by it from desire for God or that love; it does not order fruition to speculation, which would be perverse, since fruition can be ordered only to its object or more perfect fruition, God, not vision. Not both, since it has unity like geometry or arithmetic and one end, as ethics treats the soul's powers yet is practical. So it is purely practical; there is no mean for one undivided habit.
claims: Theology's principal end is charity, not truth.
Fruition cannot be ordered to speculation.
As one science, theology is purely practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2706.summary: Third: a science that is 'so that we become good' and is acquired from desire for this end is practical, and theology is so far more than ethics. Some say that, since practical is the same as operative, all knowledge operative as exemplar and preconceived rule is practical, distinguished from operative by eliciting (all habits) or instrumentally (principles of speculative science). On that view God's knowledge of things he makes is practical, wherever operative in this way, whether in the same power or another (which is material), and theology still more, as operative of love of God, its act and principal end. This is the intent of the doctors: 2 Timothy 3 ('all Scripture... that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work') and Augustine (De trinitate II: creation and Scripture exist so that God may be sought and loved).
claims: Theology aims at our becoming good more than ethics does.
Some define practical as operative by way of exemplar and rule.
Scripture and creation exist so that God may be sought and loved.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2791.summary: Objection: then one not loving God or intending to love him could not acquire theology, but many acquire it who never cared for God, and often the less devout are the subtler and deeper theologians.
claims: Many acquire theology without loving God.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2813.summary: Further objection: if theology is simply practical it perfects the practical intellect, but as the noblest acquired habit it should perfect the nobler speculative intellect, more than metaphysics; the Commentator (Ethics VI) says prudence is not the virtue of the better part as wisdom is. And faith is speculative, so theology, its science, is too. The last words begin the reply.
claims: The noblest habit should perfect the nobler speculative intellect.
Faith is speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2853.summary: Reply to the first: no one intending this science's end can acquire the habit or act of what the author calls the theology of believers and lovers, whose end is love of God. Those who called it amative or affective spoke well if they meant practical, directive of divine love (as Ovid's Ars amatoria is in its way), not a third kind. But those not moved by love of this end, content to know, can have another knowledge of the same object, of a different kind, speculative, like Aristotle's theology ordered to knowing; the saintly doctors' theology is practical. Distinct knowledges of the same object can differ in species and genus, one practical and one speculative, since they are distinguished by end, not object.
claims: Theology of believers and lovers, whose end is love of God, is practical.
Indevout scholars have a different, speculative theology of the same object.
Knowledges are distinguished by end, not object.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2903.summary: Reply to the second: our theology perfects the practical intellect. The speculative intellect is nobler, not in every act but in its highest possible act, and that perfection is the beatific vision, which the author posits as speculative theology. Our practical theology is simply nobler than any speculative science had by common law, being more immediately and perfectly ordered to that vision as the directive way. So it is false that every speculative knowledge is nobler than every practical one. Objection: of per se dividing differences one is nobler, as rational over irrational. Probably not always; it suffices that they be of opposed ratio, which avoids many difficulties.
claims: Our theology perfects the practical intellect and is nobler than any speculative science in via.
The speculative intellect's noblest perfection is the beatific vision.
Not every speculative knowledge is nobler than every practical.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e2971.summary: Reply to the third (faith): infused faith as habit is not practical, since it is not acquired or acquirable from appetite for the end; acquired explicit faith and acquired prudence (our theology) are different. So infused faith is speculative and perfects the speculative intellect. Objection: the act of believing is practical, elicited at the command of the will desiring the end, under charity's direction, since no one believes unless willing; habit and act cannot differ. Reply: an infused habit not acquired by acts can be speculative while its act is practical, though not for acquired habits. The habit of faith contributes nothing to the substance or intrinsic mode of the act, only disposing the speculative intellect to adhere firmly at the will's command; believing is not praxis (not outside cognition) though it is a practical act, and firm adherence is a passive determination of the speculative intellect by the will.
claims: Infused faith is a speculative habit, though believing is a practical act.
An infused habit can differ in character from its act.
Faith disposes the speculative intellect to firm adherence at the will's command.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3084.summary: Alternatively, faith can be called a practical but infused habit; an infused practical habit need not be acquirable from the will's desire for the end, only its act need be movable by the will, while both are required of acquired habits like our theology and acquired faith. The last words begin the reply to the principal arguments.
claims: Faith could be an infused practical habit whose act the will moves.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3104.summary: Reply to the first principal argument: Boethius takes 'theology' for metaphysics, which Aristotle also calls theology, and does not mean God is its immediate, adequate first subject, but calls God its subject because he is the noblest being under its subject, being.
claims: Boethius's 'theology' is metaphysics.
God is the noblest being under metaphysics' subject, not its adequate subject.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3122.summary: Reply to the second: theology is the noblest of all sciences had by common law, as its object shows, though practical, since it is noble for the lower to reach the higher (Politics VII), and the will is a higher power than the intellect, so it is noble for intellect to order its act to the will's act about God. Given Aristotle's view that metaphysics is noblest in via, he should have made it practical, but we need not, since metaphysics is noblest only among naturally acquirable sciences and treats the end only in general, not from love of the end. One who learned metaphysics to know God in particular from desire to love him would acquire a practical metaphysics of another kind, nobler than Aristotle's. Or: universally, the noblest science is speculative, the beatific vision or God's theology.
claims: Theology is the noblest science in via despite being practical.
The will is higher than the intellect.
Metaphysics pursued from love of God would be a different, practical science.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3206.summary: Note: Aristotle perhaps posited no practical knowledge of an eternal, necessary object like God, only of contingent doables; hence, since speculative knowledge of the necessary object is of a nobler object, he made metaphysics nobler than any practical science. We need not, since we posit practical theology of God, than which no science in via is nobler, though some speculative knowledge (not metaphysics) is simply nobler than all practical. So his argument 'science for the sake of use is less noble' fails, as does 'for the sake of knowing, therefore nobler', though each holds in some cases. Had he posited practical and speculative knowledge of the same object, he would not have so inferred.
claims: Aristotle posited no practical knowledge of necessary objects.
The inference from use to lesser nobility fails universally.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3267.summary: Reply to the third principal argument: as shown in the previous question, Aristotle's inference holds not by form nor universally; a science of eternal and immobile substance need not be speculative.
claims: Science of eternal substance need not be speculative.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3280.summary: Reply to the fourth principal argument: theology exists not for extrinsic necessities but for intrinsic ones, love of God and the ordering of morals, so it was not found once the necessities of life were had, nor presupposes them. It is practical, far more than moral philosophy, which even if found after external needs were met would still be practical, ordering morals with the end of performing the intrinsic moral good according to right reason, acquired from appetite for this end 'so that we become good'. Theology likewise presupposes sufficient external necessities, and distraction by them impedes study, but it is practical, for intrinsic necessities. Aristotle could not say this of his metaphysics, ordered to nothing necessary. This concludes the prologue questions.
claims: Theology exists for intrinsic necessities, love of God and ordering of morals.
Theology is practical even though external necessities are presupposed for study.

qrdBas-a19815-d1e3337.summary: Heading introducing Bassolis's commentary on the first distinction of Book 1, following the prologue questions.

qrdBas-a19815.summary: Prologue q8 asks whether theology is practical or speculative. Bassolis surveys five opinions. He rejects three ways of holding theology purely speculative. The first says the will's act toward the end needs no direction, but he replies that the end in particular can be willed wrongly. The second says love of God is not praxis because its object is not contingent, but it meets all the conditions of praxis. The third says only commanded acts or acts following choice are praxis, but choice itself, generating virtue even when wholly interior, is praxis. Against the Scotist view that theology is simply practical from its object (God virtually containing the rectitude of praxis, with aptitudinal priority and conformity), he objects that no object makes knowledge practical. Aptitudinal relations cannot make knowledge actually practical, and the criterion would make God's self-knowledge and Metaphysics XII practical, whereas the same object can be known both ways, like the geometer's and the carpenter's straight line. Against Aquinas (theology one yet both, more speculative because ordered to vision), he holds that a finite habit cannot be both, that Aquinas inconsistently names revealability as the subject's ratio, and that beatitude lies principally in love and fruition, not vision. Against the view that theology is speculative and practical by its parts, he argues that every part serves to direct praxis. 'Neither', 'affective', and 'contemplative' are not further members. His answer: God's theology and the blessed's are purely speculative, since no error is possible in God's will or in beatific love, so their knowledge is ostensive rather than directive. Possible abstractive theology is speculative if wholly infused, practical if its acts can be moved by desire to direct fallible love. Our theology, acquired by study from love of God to direct charity, is simply practical as a whole and is nobler than any naturally had speculative science. Indevout scholars have a different, speculative theology of the same object, since knowledges differ by end, not object. Infused faith is a speculative habit whose act, believing at the will's command, is practical. Aristotle's linking of nobility with speculation fails because he knew no practical science of a necessary object. The item ends with the heading to Book 1, distinction 1.
claims: God's and the blessed's theology are purely speculative because their will cannot err, so their knowledge is ostensive, not directive.
Our theology, acquired from love of God to direct charitable love, is simply practical as a whole.
Knowledge is practical from its end (appetite for the end), not its object; the same object admits practical and speculative knowledge.
Love of God and choice are true praxis.
Our practical theology is nobler than any speculative science naturally available in via; beatitude consists principally in love.
Infused faith is a speculative habit whose act is practical.
